Justice Adefope-Okojie said the judiciary must stop determining who occupies elective offices when the people’s choice cannot be established, stressing that courts should correct electoral injustices rather than substitute their decisions for the will of voters.
The retired Justice spoke on Tuesday while delivering the 2026 GAVEL International Annual Lecture, titled, “Electoral Process in Nigeria: Managing the Boundaries of Judicial Intervention.”

She maintained that where a candidate’s disqualification or other electoral defects made it impossible to establish the actual winner, the appropriate remedy should ordinarily be a fresh election rather than declaring the runner-up elected.
“It is not the duty of the Courts to award seats,” she declared, warning that electoral adjudication must not become an alternative route through which politicians acquire mandates they could not secure at the polls.
The retired jurist said Nigeria’s electoral system has increasingly turned the judiciary into an arbiter of political power, with candidates and political parties relying heavily on litigation to determine electoral outcomes.
To illustrate the scale of the problem, she disclosed that 1,209 petitions were filed after the 2023 general elections in respect of 1,280 contested elective positions, representing approximately 94.5 petitions for every 100 seats.
By comparison, she said Kenya recorded 6.5 petitions per 100 elective seats in its 2022 elections, while Ghana recorded 5.8 in 2020.
Of the 1,209 petitions filed in Nigeria, only 103 succeeded, a development she said raised serious questions about public confidence in the country’s electoral process.
Blaming political parties for much of the litigation, Justice Adefope-Okojie identified flawed congresses, the imposition of candidates and the unlawful substitution of duly elected aspirants as major sources of electoral disputes.
She consequently urged courts to abandon their reluctance to intervene in the internal affairs of political parties when they violate their constitutions and electoral laws.
Citing the Supreme Court’s 30 April 2026 decision in PDP v. Sule Lamido, she said the judiciary must not allow political parties to exploit the doctrine of non-justiciability of internal party affairs to perpetrate injustice.
The jurist also criticised the stringent evidential requirements imposed on petitioners, particularly the insistence that electoral officials and witnesses from individual polling units must testify before certified electoral documents can be admitted or relied upon.
She argued that such requirements placed an almost impossible burden on petitioners and could prevent courts from examining credible evidence of electoral manipulation.
With the 2027 general elections approaching, she urged judges and election tribunal members to demonstrate integrity, impartiality and transparency in handling electoral disputes.
She said the ultimate test of a good election judgment should be whether the person occupying an elective office was actually chosen by the lawful votes cast, or whether the matter had been returned to voters where their choice could not be established.
“The Constitution places sovereignty in the people and makes the Courts the guardians of that sovereignty, not its holders,” she said.
She added that a judgment correcting a stolen mandate honours the people’s choice, while one conferring a mandate the electorate never gave diminishes it.
“The final aim of electoral adjudication should be its own decline: a democracy in which elections are won and lost at the ballot box, not in the courtroom,” she said.
Also speaking at the event, human rights lawyer Femi Falana (SAN) called for a review of Nigeria’s electoral litigation system, accusing the National Assembly of creating a judicial arrangement that unnecessarily burdens the Supreme Court with election appeals.
Falana urged the judiciary and lawmakers to restore the previous legal framework for determining governorship election disputes, which he said would ease the Supreme Court’s workload.
He recalled that attempts to reverse the arrangement since 2011 had repeatedly failed, despite concerns over the volume of election-related cases reaching the apex court.
The Senior Advocate also criticised what he described as discriminatory differences in the appellate procedures for presidential and legislative election petitions, arguing that the existing arrangement lacked justification.
Recalling controversial electoral judgments, including cases in Kogi and Zamfara, Falana lamented that judicial decisions had sometimes displaced voters’ choices and installed candidates who did not win at the polls.
Gavel International publisher Mustapha Ogunsakin praised retired Justice Oludotun Adefope-Okojie for her leadership and courage, recalling her role on a tribunal the Lagos State Government established to investigate security incidents at the state High Court in Ikeja in 2005.
He said Justice Adefope-Okojie showed exceptional leadership, intellectual depth, and fearlessness, ensuring differing opinions were considered and the tribunal completed its assignment within the stipulated period.
According to Ogunsakin, the tribunal’s recommendations provided a lasting framework for improving security at court premises across Lagos State and earned commendation from then-Governor Bola Tinubu.
